title: Short Stuff: Botox Brain
summary: Short Stuff episode (Josh filling in for Dave Crowder-style sign-off banter) on Botox and the brain. Covers what Botox is (botulinum toxin, made by Clostridium botulinum, the most potent known neurotoxin), its medical history from the 1970s with Dr. Alan B. Scott treating strabismus, its cosmetic use from the 2000s to smooth glabellar wrinkles, and the loss of facial expression it causes. It then explains the facial feedback hypothesis and reports research finding that Botox injections in the glabellar region (between the brows) reduce amygdala activity, alleviating depression symptoms, and possibly borderline personality disorder, confirmed with fMRI scans. A comparison with acupuncture is noted, and the hosts mention Botox for migraines and hopes for coverage for depression, BPD, and anxiety.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction
segments.summary: Josh introduces the Short Stuff episode, with light jokes about the title, Pinky and the Brain, and Botox in the Brain.

segments.title: What Botox is and botulism
segments.summary: Josh explains that Botox is a brand of botulinum toxin, produced by Clostridium botulinum, which he calls the most potent known neurotoxin. He describes how it blocks acetylcholine release at nerve endings, causing paralysis.

segments.title: Medical history of Botox
segments.summary: Chuck says Botox was used medically starting in the 1970s when Dr. Alan B. Scott proposed treating strabismus, and the FDA agreed. Cosmetic use took off in the 2000s, smoothing forehead wrinkles for about three months.

segments.title: Botox and loss of facial expression
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck discuss how Botox paralyzes the muscles that form wrinkles, leaving the face unable to show emotion for three to four months, and how this can look creepy.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: The hosts take a break before the main reveal.

segments.title: Facial feedback hypothesis
segments.summary: Chuck explains the facial feedback hypothesis: mimicking others' expressions can shape our moods, and expressions can influence emotions in both directions. Josh notes that people had assumed feelings drive expressions, not the reverse.

segments.title: Botox as a depression and BPD treatment
segments.summary: Patients reported reduced depression after Botox injections in the glabellar region. Researchers linked this to the amygdala, using fMRI scans to show altered amygdala activity in depressed patients and in people with borderline personality disorder. Josh says the indirect action on the amygdala makes it safer than drugs acting directly on it.

segments.title: Acupuncture comparison and other uses
segments.summary: The hosts note that an acupuncture comparison group improved clinically but did not show the neurological effect seen with Botox. They mention Botox's use for anxiety and migraines, with insurance covering migraine treatment.

segments.title: Listener tip credit
segments.summary: Josh credits his wife for tipping him off to the topic and the hosts sign off the segment.

segments.title: Sign-off and credits
segments.summary: Chuck closes with the production credit and directs listeners to the iHeartRadio app and podcast platforms.
